title: The Library's Borrowed Energy
passage:
The public library in Aoba City was proud of staying open until nine in the evening. Students used the quiet desks after school, workers stopped by on their way home, and parents brought children to the reading room after dinner. However, the library's electricity use was highest during the final three hours of the day, even though fewer people were inside. The city asked the staff to look for ways to reduce energy use without shortening opening hours.

At first, several people suggested turning off half the lights after six. The building manager warned that a simple cut might make some shelves too dark and could create safety problems. Instead, the staff spent one week measuring how different parts of the building were actually used. They discovered that the second-floor reference area was nearly empty after seven, while the first-floor study tables remained busy. They also found that lights in meeting rooms stayed on even when the rooms had not been reserved.

The library tested a more flexible system. After seven, the reference area remained available, but only the lights near occupied tables stayed bright. Motion sensors were added to two meeting-room corridors, and staff members checked unused rooms during their evening rounds. The heating and cooling system was also adjusted so that empty sections were not kept at exactly the same temperature as crowded ones.

The changes saved electricity, but a new issue appeared. Some visitors said that the darker second floor made the library feel as if it were closing. Even though the space was still open, people hesitated to walk upstairs. The staff responded by keeping the entrance to the second floor brightly lit and adding a clear sign explaining that the area remained available. They also placed small desk lamps at individual tables.

After three months, the city compared electricity use with the same period from the previous year. The library had used about twelve percent less power during evening hours. More importantly, visitor numbers had not fallen. The project taught the staff that energy efficiency was not only a technical problem. People react to spaces emotionally as well as practically. A room can be safe enough according to a light meter and still feel unwelcoming. The successful plan worked because it combined measured energy savings with attention to how visitors experienced the building. The library did not have to choose between staying open and using less power. It had to understand where energy was needed most and make the quieter parts of the building respond to actual use.
translation:
青葉市の公共図書館は午後九時まで開館していることを大切にしていました。放課後の学生、仕事帰りの会社員、夕食後に子どもを連れてくる保護者などが利用していました。しかし利用者が少なくなる最後の三時間に電力使用量が高いことが分かり、市は開館時間を短くせず節電する方法を求めました。

最初は午後六時以降、照明を半分消す案が出ました。しかし単純に消すと棚が暗くなり安全上の問題が出る可能性があります。そこで一週間、建物のどこが実際に使われているか調べました。二階の参考資料エリアは七時以降ほぼ空きますが、一階の学習席は混雑したままでした。また、予約のない会議室の照明が点灯していることも分かりました。

図書館はより柔軟な方法を試しました。七時以降も二階は利用可能ですが、人がいる机周辺だけ明るくし、会議室前には人感センサーを設置しました。空いている区画は混雑区画と同じ温度に保たないよう空調も調整しました。

節電効果はありましたが、新しい問題も生まれました。二階が暗くなると、実際には開いていても『閉館しそう』に感じる利用者がいたのです。そこで二階入口は明るく保ち、利用可能であることを示す案内を置き、個別机には小さなランプも用意しました。

三か月後、前年同時期と比べると夜間の電力使用は約十二パーセント減っていました。利用者数は減っていませんでした。この計画から、節電は技術だけの問題ではないと分かりました。照度計では安全でも、人には歓迎されていないように感じる空間があります。成功したのは、数値としての節電と、利用者が空間をどう感じるかの両方を考えたからです。図書館は『開館を続けるか節電するか』を選ぶ必要はなく、どこにエネルギーが本当に必要なのかを理解すればよかったのです。

title: A Garden Under the Highway
passage:
A wide highway crossed above a neighborhood in Nishi Ward. Under the road was a strip of land that received little direct sunlight. For many years, it was used only for bicycle parking and storage. The ground was mostly concrete, and residents thought plants would not grow there. When the city asked for ideas to make the area more pleasant, a local gardening group proposed an experiment rather than a complete redesign.

The group began by studying the light. They measured brightness at different hours and found that the eastern end received two hours of morning sun, while the center remained shaded all day. They also checked where rainwater collected and discovered that one corner stayed damp after storms. Instead of choosing the same plant for the whole space, they selected species for different conditions. Herbs that needed more light went to the eastern end, while ferns and other shade-loving plants were placed near the center.

The first planting was small. The group used large containers rather than breaking the concrete. This made the experiment cheaper and easier to change. Residents donated pots, and a nearby restaurant provided clean buckets that could be reused. A narrow walking path was left open so bicycle users would not have to move around the garden.

Within two months, some plants were doing well, but others were weak. The highway blocked not only sunlight but also some rain, so containers that looked damp on the surface were dry underneath. Volunteers changed the watering schedule. They also noticed that noise from traffic made the area unpleasant for long conversations. Instead of adding benches everywhere, they created only one small seating area at the quietest edge.

By autumn, the space had not become a traditional garden. Traffic still passed overhead, and the concrete remained visible. Yet the area felt less empty. People stopped to smell herbs, children looked for insects, and the restaurant sometimes used a small amount of mint from the containers. The project succeeded because the group did not begin with an image of what a perfect garden should look like. They began with the actual conditions: shade, noise, water, movement, and cost. The unusual site could support life, but only if the design respected what the site could and could not provide. Residents learned that improvement does not always mean hiding difficult conditions. Sometimes it means working honestly with them.
translation:
西区のある地域には高速道路が高架で通り、その下にほとんど直射日光の当たらない細長い土地がありました。長年、自転車置き場や物置としてしか使われず、地面はほぼコンクリートだったため、住民は植物を育てる場所ではないと考えていました。市が改善案を募集すると、地域の園芸グループは全面改修ではなく小さな実験を提案しました。

まず時間帯ごとの明るさを測ると、東端は朝に二時間ほど日が当たり、中央は一日中日陰でした。雨水がたまる場所も調べ、嵐の後に湿ったままになる角を見つけました。同じ植物を全体へ植えるのではなく、明るい場所には日光を好むハーブ、中央にはシダなど日陰を好む植物を選びました。

コンクリートを壊さず大きな鉢を使うことで費用を抑え、失敗しても配置を変えられるようにしました。住民から鉢を集め、近くの飲食店からは洗浄済みのバケツを提供してもらいました。自転車利用者の通路も残しました。

二か月後、元気な植物もあれば弱るものもありました。高速道路は日光だけでなく雨も遮るため、表面が湿って見えても下が乾いている鉢があったのです。水やり方法を直し、交通騒音が大きいことも考えて、ベンチは最も静かな端に一か所だけ置きました。

秋になっても、そこは普通の庭にはなりませんでした。頭上では車が走り、コンクリートも見えます。それでも空虚な場所ではなくなりました。ハーブの香りを楽しむ人、虫を探す子ども、少量のミントを使う飲食店も現れました。成功の理由は『理想の庭』から始めず、日陰、騒音、水、人の動き、費用という実際の条件から考えたことでした。難しい条件を隠すのではなく、その条件と正直に付き合うことでも場所は改善できるのです。

title: The Two-Minute Delay
passage:
The local train from Minato Station was scheduled to leave at 7:18 every morning. Commuters trusted the time because the train connected with a faster service at Central Station. For several weeks in spring, however, the train often left two or three minutes late. The delay seemed small, but some passengers missed the connection and had to wait fifteen minutes for the next train.

The railway company first assumed that boarding was simply taking longer because more people were traveling. Staff members counted passengers and found that the number had increased only slightly. They then watched what happened on the platform. The problem turned out to be concentrated near one door. A new staircase had opened beside the platform, and many passengers entered at the same place. They formed a crowd around the closest train door while other doors had shorter lines.

The company could have added staff every morning, but that would have been expensive. Instead, they tried changing the signs. Large floor marks showed passengers where the less crowded doors stopped. An electronic screen near the staircase displayed a message asking riders to spread along the platform. For the first few days, staff members also stood nearby and explained the new system.

The change helped, but it did not remove the delay completely. Some passengers still preferred the nearest door because it was closest to the escalator at Central Station. The railway company realized that passengers were not behaving irrationally. They were choosing a door that made the next part of their trip easier. The company therefore added information showing which doors were closest to stairs and exits at the destination. This allowed people to choose deliberately instead of crowding the same place without knowing the alternatives.

Within a month, average departure delay dropped to less than one minute. The result came from looking carefully at a small problem. Two minutes did not sound important when viewed by itself, but the effect became larger because of the connection fifteen minutes later. The company also learned that telling people to ‘spread out’ was less effective than understanding why they gathered in one place. Good solutions often depend on seeing the whole journey, not only the moment when the problem becomes visible.
translation:
港駅を毎朝7時18分に出る普通列車は、中央駅で快速へ接続するため、多くの通勤客が時刻を頼りにしていました。ところが春の数週間、二、三分遅れて発車することが増えました。わずかな遅れに見えても、接続を逃すと次の列車まで十五分待たなければならない人がいました。

鉄道会社は最初、利用者増加で乗車に時間がかかっていると考えました。しかし人数はわずかしか増えていませんでした。ホームを観察すると、新しい階段のすぐ近くの一つの扉に乗客が集中していることが分かりました。他の扉は空いていても、階段から来た人が最寄りの扉に集まっていたのです。

毎朝係員を増やす代わりに、床へ大きな乗車位置表示を付け、電子表示でホーム全体へ広がるよう案内しました。最初の数日は係員も説明しました。

それでも一部の人は中央駅のエスカレーターに近い扉を選び続けました。これは不合理ではなく、次の移動を楽にするための選択でした。そこで鉄道会社は、到着駅の階段や出口に近い車両位置も表示しました。乗客は同じ場所へ無意識に集まるのではなく、目的に応じて選べるようになりました。

一か月後、平均遅延は一分未満になりました。二分という小さな問題も、その先の十五分待ちにつながれば影響は大きくなります。また『散らばってください』と命令するより、なぜ人が一か所へ集まるのか理解する方が効果的でした。問題が見える一瞬だけでなく、旅全体を見ることが良い解決につながる場合があります。

title: A Store That Closed at Noon
passage:
A small grocery store in a mountain village had been open from eight in the morning until seven in the evening for more than thirty years. The owner, Mr. Seki, was getting older and found the long day difficult. The village depended on the shop for basic food, especially residents who did not drive. Mr. Seki considered closing the business completely, but the community asked whether there was another option.

For one month, the village council recorded when customers actually visited. They discovered two busy periods: early morning and late afternoon. Between noon and three, only a few people entered the store. The council suggested closing for three hours in the middle of the day. Mr. Seki could rest, receive deliveries, and complete paperwork during that time.

Some residents disliked the idea at first. They worried that visitors would arrive during the closed period and assume the store had gone out of business. Others said workers with unusual schedules sometimes shopped at lunchtime. The council did not ignore these concerns. They created a clear sign showing the new hours and placed the same information at the bus stop and village website. A refrigerated locker was also installed beside the store so customers could collect pre-ordered food while the shop was closed.

The new schedule began in June. At first, Mr. Seki felt uncomfortable locking the door at noon because he had never done so. After several weeks, however, he said he was less tired in the evening. Customers quickly learned the new hours. A few people used the locker, and others changed the time of their shopping. Total weekly sales fell only slightly, while Mr. Seki's working hours dropped by eighteen hours per week.

The experiment did not solve every long-term problem. The village still needed to think about who would run the shop in the future. Yet the midday closure gave everyone more time to plan. The community learned that keeping an important service does not always mean keeping it exactly the same. If the old form becomes impossible, a smaller change may preserve the part that matters most. In this case, three closed hours helped prevent seven closed days.
translation:
山間の村にある小さな食料品店は、三十年以上、朝八時から夜七時まで営業していました。店主の関さんは高齢になり、長時間営業がつらくなっていました。車を運転しない住民にとって生活に必要な店だったため、完全閉店を考えた関さんに、地域は別の方法がないか尋ねました。

一か月間、実際に客が来る時間を記録すると、朝と夕方が混み、正午から三時まではほとんど客が来ないことが分かりました。そこで昼の三時間を閉め、休憩、仕入れの受け取り、事務作業へ使う案が出ました。

当初は、観光客が閉店した店だと誤解することや、昼休みに買う人が困ることを心配する声もありました。新営業時間を大きく表示し、バス停と村のウェブサイトにも掲載しました。また、店が閉まっている間でも予約商品を受け取れる冷蔵ロッカーを設置しました。

六月から新しい時間で営業すると、関さんは最初、正午に鍵をかけることへ抵抗を感じました。しかし数週間後には夕方の疲れが減りました。客もすぐ慣れ、一部はロッカーを使い、他の人は買い物時間を変えました。週売上はわずかに下がりましたが、関さんの労働時間は週十八時間も減りました。

将来だれが店を継ぐかという問題は残っています。それでも昼休業によって考える時間が生まれました。大切なサービスを守ることは、昔と全く同じ形を守ることではありません。従来の形が続けられないなら、重要な部分を残すために形を小さく変える方法があります。この村では、一日三時間閉めることが、週七日すべて閉まることを防いだのです。

title: The Rainwater Tank
passage:
The sports club at a suburban school used a large amount of tap water during summer. Students washed muddy equipment, watered the field edges, and cleaned outdoor benches. After a dry year, the school began looking for simple ways to reduce water use. A science teacher suggested collecting rainwater from the roof of the equipment shed.

The first plan was ambitious. Some students wanted to install a very large tank so the club could avoid tap water almost completely. The school engineer explained that a full tank would be extremely heavy and would need a strong foundation. Rainfall was also irregular. A giant tank could still be empty after several dry weeks. The group decided to begin with a smaller system that could be evaluated safely.

A gutter directed roof water into a covered tank. A screen kept leaves and insects out, and the first dirty water after a long dry period was sent away from the tank. The collected water was clearly labeled as non-drinking water. Students could use it for cleaning and plants, but not for washing hands or filling bottles.

During the rainy season, the tank filled quickly. Students enjoyed using the stored water and sometimes competed to see which team could finish cleaning with the least amount. In August, however, rainfall decreased and the tank often became empty. This was not considered a failure. The project had never promised an endless supply. Its purpose was to replace tap water when rainwater was available.

At the end of the term, the science class compared meter readings with those from the previous year. Outdoor tap-water use had fallen by about twenty percent. The number varied from month to month, depending on rainfall. The school decided to keep the tank and later add a second one near the gardening area.

Students learned that environmental projects need realistic expectations. A useful system does not have to solve one hundred percent of a problem. The rainwater tank worked because it had a limited, clear role. It used a resource that would otherwise flow into a drain, while tap water remained available when needed. The value came from combining the two sources rather than pretending one could completely replace the other.
translation:
郊外の学校の運動部では、夏に多くの水道水を使っていました。泥の付いた道具を洗い、グラウンド周辺へ水をやり、屋外ベンチを掃除するためです。雨の少ない年を経験した後、学校は節水方法を考え、理科の先生が用具倉庫の屋根から雨水を集める案を出しました。

最初、生徒たちは巨大なタンクを置き、水道をほぼ使わなくしたいと考えました。しかし満水時の重量には強い基礎が必要で、雨量も一定ではありません。大きなタンクでも何週間も雨がなければ空になります。そこで安全に評価できる小型設備から始めました。

雨どいからふた付きタンクへ水を入れ、網で葉や虫を防ぎ、長い晴天後の最初の汚れた水はタンクへ入れないようにしました。飲料不可と明示し、掃除や植物には使えますが、手洗いや飲み水には使わないルールにしました。

梅雨にはすぐ満水になりましたが、八月は雨が減り空になる日も増えました。それは失敗とは考えませんでした。無限に水を供給する計画ではなく、雨水がある時だけ水道水の代わりに使うのが目的だったからです。

学期末に前年のメーター記録と比べると、屋外の水道水使用量は約二十パーセント減っていました。効果は雨量によって月ごとに違いましたが、学校は設備を残し、園芸区画にも二つ目を追加することにしました。

生徒たちは、環境対策は問題の百パーセントを解決しなくても価値があると学びました。このタンクは『雨水がある時に使う』という限定された役割だからこそ機能しました。一つの資源で全部を置き換えるのではなく、二つを組み合わせることに意味があったのです。

title: A School Newspaper Correction
passage:
The school newspaper at Seiran Junior High published an article about the upcoming cultural festival. The article said that the drama club would perform on Saturday at two o'clock. The information came from an early planning sheet. After the newspaper had been printed, the drama club noticed that the performance had actually been moved to three o'clock.

The student editors were embarrassed. They had checked spelling and names carefully, but nobody had confirmed the final schedule. One editor suggested quietly changing the time on the online version and saying nothing about the printed mistake. Another student disagreed. Hundreds of paper copies had already been distributed, so many readers would never see the silent change.

The group decided to publish a clear correction. They placed a small notice near the school entrance, posted the corrected time online, and added a message to the morning school announcement. The next issue of the newspaper also included a short note explaining the error. The note did not blame the drama club or the student who wrote the original article. It simply stated that the newspaper had used an older schedule and should have checked the final version.

Some editors worried that admitting the mistake would make readers trust the newspaper less. Their teacher argued that the opposite could happen if corrections were handled openly. No newspaper could promise never to make an error. What mattered was how quickly mistakes were identified, corrected, and prevented from happening again.

The group changed its process. Articles about dates, prices, or schedules now had to be checked against an official source on the final editing day. One student was assigned to mark facts that could change. The system added a few minutes to production, but it reduced the chance of repeating the same type of error.

On festival day, the drama performance began at three, and the audience was full. The incorrect article did not cause a serious problem because the correction reached most readers in time. The student editors learned that accuracy is not only about being right the first time. It also includes being willing to say clearly when something was wrong and showing what will be done differently afterward.
translation:
青嵐中学校の学校新聞は文化祭の記事で、演劇部の上演が土曜日の二時からだと掲載しました。その情報は初期の計画表から取ったものでした。印刷後、演劇部から実際には三時へ変更されていると連絡がありました。

編集部は恥ずかしく感じました。名前や誤字はよく確認したのに、最終日程を確認していなかったのです。オンライン版だけ黙って直そうという意見も出ましたが、紙はすでに何百部も配られており、多くの読者には修正が届きません。

そこで学校入口へ訂正掲示を出し、オンライン版を直し、朝の校内放送でも正しい時刻を知らせました。次号には短い訂正文を載せ、演劇部や記事を書いた生徒を責めず、『古い日程を使い、最終版確認が不足していた』と説明しました。

間違いを認めると新聞への信頼が下がるのではと心配する生徒もいました。しかし先生は、公開して直す方が信頼につながる場合があると言いました。絶対に間違えない新聞はありません。重要なのは、間違いをどれだけ早く見つけ、直し、同じことを防ぐかです。

その後、日付、料金、時刻など変わり得る情報は最終編集日に公式資料と照合し、変更可能な事実に印を付ける担当も決めました。作業は少し増えましたが、同じ種類の失敗を減らせます。

文化祭当日、演劇は三時から満員の観客の前で始まりました。訂正が間に合ったため大きな混乱はありませんでした。編集部は、正確さとは最初から正しいことだけではなく、間違った時には明確に認め、その後どう変えるか示すことも含むと学びました。

title: The Bicycle Count
passage:
A city planned to build a new bicycle parking area near a busy shopping street. Shop owners supported the idea because bicycles were often left beside sidewalks. However, the city had to decide how large the parking area should be. Building too few spaces would leave the problem unsolved, while building too many would use land that could serve another purpose.

A local high school geography class offered to help collect data. For two weeks, students counted bicycles at four locations three times a day: before school, at lunchtime, and in the early evening. They also recorded weather because rain might affect bicycle use. At first, the work seemed repetitive, but students soon saw why consistent timing mattered. A count at ten in the morning could not fairly be compared with a count at six in the evening.

The data showed that the busiest period was not lunchtime, as many shop owners had guessed. Bicycle numbers were highest between five and six, when students and workers stopped at the shopping street on their way home. Saturdays were different again, with a wider spread of use from late morning to afternoon. Rainy days had far fewer bicycles.

The class also noticed that some bicycles remained in the same place for several days. Those bicycles were not part of ordinary short-term shopping demand. The city decided to contact owners and create a separate rule for long-term abandoned bicycles. Without making that distinction, the parking estimate would have been too high.

Using the student data, planners designed a parking area with fewer spaces than first proposed but left room for future expansion. They also placed a small temporary rack nearby during the opening month to see whether demand exceeded expectations. It did not.

The students were pleased that their simple counts affected a real decision. They learned that collecting data is not only about producing a large number. The way a question is defined matters. When should something be counted? Which cases belong in the count? What outside conditions might change the result? The bicycles had been visible to everyone for years, but careful observation turned a general impression of ‘too many bicycles’ into information that could guide a practical choice.
translation:
市は商店街近くに新しい自転車置き場を作る計画を立てました。歩道に自転車が並ぶことが多かったため店主も賛成しましたが、問題は必要な規模です。小さすぎれば問題が残り、大きすぎれば他に使える土地を無駄にします。

地元高校の地理クラスが二週間、四か所で一日三回、自転車数を数えました。登校前、昼、夕方に同じ時刻で測り、雨天かどうかも記録しました。時間をそろえなければ、公平に比較できないことがすぐ分かりました。

店主の多くは昼が最も混むと思っていましたが、実際は学生や会社員が帰宅途中に立ち寄る午後五時から六時が最多でした。土曜日は昼前から午後まで広く利用され、雨の日は大幅に減りました。

さらに数日間同じ場所に置かれた自転車もありました。これは通常の短時間利用とは別に扱う必要があります。放置自転車を含めれば必要台数を過大評価してしまうため、市は別の対応ルールを作りました。

データを基に、当初案より少ない台数で設計しつつ、将来拡張できる空間を残しました。開設後一か月は仮設ラックも置きましたが、予想を超える需要はありませんでした。

生徒たちは、単純な『数える作業』が実際の政策判断へつながったことを喜びました。データ収集では大きな数字を作ることより、何をいつ数えるのか、どの例を含めるのか、天候など何が結果を変えるのかを決めることが重要です。何年も見えていた『自転車が多い』という印象が、丁寧な観察によって具体的な判断材料へ変わりました。

title: The Museum Without Labels
passage:
A small history museum decided to redesign one room for a special weekend. Instead of placing long labels beside every object, the staff removed almost all written explanations. Visitors saw an old lunch box, a hand-operated sewing machine, a school bag, and several tools, but they were not told immediately what each object was used for. The experiment was meant to encourage closer observation.

At the entrance, visitors received a card with three questions: What do you notice? What do you think this object was used for? What makes you think so? Staff members were nearby to help, but they waited until visitors had looked carefully before giving answers. Children especially enjoyed guessing. One group thought a metal tool was part of a musical instrument. Another child correctly noticed that a worn wooden handle suggested the tool had been held many times.

Not everyone liked the room. Some adults said they came to a museum to learn facts, not to guess. A visitor who had limited time wanted clear information immediately. The staff realized that curiosity and access to information should not be treated as opposites. Halfway through the weekend, they added small cards that could be turned over. The front asked an observation question; the back provided the name, date, and explanation.

This change improved the experience. Visitors who enjoyed guessing could wait before turning the card, while others could read the information at once. Staff also noticed that people spent more time discussing objects with family members. The conversation often continued even after the correct answer was revealed because visitors wanted to compare their first ideas with the historical explanation.

After the weekend, the museum did not remove labels from all its rooms. Detailed information remained important, especially for complex topics. However, the staff changed several displays so that a short question appeared before the explanation. The experiment showed them that museums can offer more than facts. They can also help visitors practice looking carefully, forming ideas from evidence, and then revising those ideas when new information appears. The best display was not necessarily the one that said the most words first. Sometimes learning began with a well-placed question.
translation:
ある小さな歴史博物館は、特別な週末に一室の展示方法を変えました。すべての物の横に長い説明を置くのではなく、ほとんどのラベルを外しました。古い弁当箱、手回しミシン、通学かばん、工具などが並びますが、何に使った物かはすぐには示しません。来館者にまずよく観察してもらう実験でした。

入口で『何に気づいたか』『何に使ったと思うか』『なぜそう思うか』という三つの問いが書かれたカードを渡しました。職員は近くにいましたが、観察が終わるまで答えを教えません。特に子どもたちは推理を楽しみ、木の持ち手のすり減りから頻繁に使われた道具だと考える子もいました。

一方、全員が楽しんだわけではありません。『博物館には事実を学びに来たのであって、当て物をしに来たのではない』という大人もおり、時間のない人はすぐ説明を読みたがりました。そこで職員は、表に問い、裏に名称・年代・説明を書いた小さなカードを追加しました。

これにより、考えたい人は裏返さずに観察し、すぐ情報が必要な人はすぐ読めるようになりました。家族同士で物について話す時間も増え、正解を知った後も最初の考えと歴史的説明を比べて会話が続きました。

博物館はすべてのラベルを廃止したわけではありません。複雑な内容では詳しい説明が不可欠です。ただし一部展示では説明の前に短い問いを置くようになりました。この実験から、博物館は事実を伝えるだけでなく、よく観察し、証拠から考え、新しい情報で考えを修正する練習の場にもなれると分かりました。学びは、最初から最も多くの言葉を見せることではなく、良い問いから始まることもあります。

title: The Extra Step in the Recipe
passage:
In a home economics class, students were asked to make vegetable soup from the same basic recipe. The instructions listed ingredients, amounts, and cooking times. Most groups followed the steps exactly. One group, however, added an extra step: they tasted the soup before adding the final amount of salt. Their soup needed less salt than the recipe suggested because the stock they had used was already salty.

The teacher used the example to begin a discussion about instructions. A recipe is designed to make a result more reliable, but ingredients are not always identical. Tomatoes can be sweeter or more sour, onions can vary in size, and different brands of stock contain different amounts of salt. Following instructions carefully is important, but so is checking what is actually happening.

The next week, the class repeated the soup lesson with one change. Each group received vegetables of slightly different sizes. Students had to decide whether the written cooking time still made sense. One group cut large carrots into smaller pieces so they would cook at the same speed as potatoes. Another group kept the pieces large and simply cooked them longer. Both approaches worked.

The lesson was not meant to encourage students to ignore recipes. Beginners often need clear instructions because they do not yet know which changes are safe. The teacher explained that flexibility should grow from observation, not random guessing. A student who changes five things at once may not understand why the result improves or becomes worse.

Students wrote notes beside the recipe: ‘taste before final salt,’ ‘check vegetable softness,’ and ‘change one thing at a time.’ These notes turned a fixed set of instructions into a guide that included moments for judgment.

By the end of the unit, many students saw recipes differently. A recipe was not a command that removed the need to think. It was a tested starting point. The extra step of tasting the soup was small, but it represented an important skill: using a plan while still paying attention to the real situation. The same idea could apply beyond cooking. Instructions are most useful when people understand both when to follow them closely and when evidence shows that a careful adjustment is needed.
translation:
家庭科の授業で、生徒たちは同じ基本レシピを使って野菜スープを作りました。材料、量、加熱時間が示され、多くの班がその通りに進めました。ところが一つの班だけ、最後の塩を入れる前に味見をしました。使ったスープストック自体に塩分が多かったため、レシピより少ない塩で十分でした。

先生はこの例から『手順』について話しました。レシピは結果を安定させるためのものですが、材料はいつも同じではありません。トマトの甘さや酸味、玉ねぎの大きさ、スープストックの塩分は変わります。指示を丁寧に守ることも大切ですが、実際に何が起きているか確かめることも必要です。

翌週、少しずつ大きさの違う野菜を各班へ配り、記載された加熱時間がそのまま使えるか考えさせました。大きいニンジンを小さく切る班もあれば、大きいまま長く煮る班もあり、どちらも成功しました。

これはレシピを無視する授業ではありません。初心者には安全で明確な手順が必要です。先生は、柔軟さは適当な思いつきではなく観察から生まれるべきだと説明しました。一度に五つ変えると、何が結果へ影響したのか分かりません。

生徒たちはレシピの横へ『最後の塩の前に味見』『野菜の柔らかさを確認』『変更は一度に一つ』と書き込みました。固定された指示が、判断する場面を含むガイドへ変わりました。

学習の最後、生徒たちはレシピを『考えなくてよい命令』ではなく、『試されてきた出発点』として見るようになりました。味見という小さな一手間は、計画を使いながら現実にも注意を向けるという大切な技能を表しています。この考え方は料理以外にも当てはまります。

title: The Tree at the Bus Stop
passage:
At a busy bus stop near a hospital, people often waited in direct sunlight during summer. There was a narrow roof over part of the stop, but it provided little shade in the late afternoon when the sun came from the west. The city considered installing a larger metal shelter. Before construction began, a landscape planner asked whether a tree could provide part of the solution.

The idea sounded attractive, but planting a tree was not as simple as placing one in the ground. Underground pipes limited where roots could grow. A very large tree might block signs or damage the pavement. A small tree would take years to provide useful shade. The planner studied several species and chose one that grew moderately fast, could handle city heat, and had roots less likely to lift the sidewalk.

The city still built a smaller shelter because people needed shade immediately. The tree was planted several meters west of the waiting area so that, as it grew, its afternoon shadow would fall toward the seats. A protective frame kept bicycles from damaging the young trunk. During the first two summers, city workers watered it regularly.

Some residents complained that spending money on a tree made little sense because the shelter already existed. Others liked the tree but expected it to cool the stop immediately. The planner explained that the project worked on two time scales. The shelter solved today's problem. The tree was an investment in future shade, cooler pavement, and a more pleasant street.

Five years later, the tree was large enough to cast a broad shadow over part of the waiting area. On hot afternoons, people often chose seats under the leaves rather than under the metal roof. The temperature difference was not dramatic every day, but the space felt more comfortable, and birds occasionally rested in the branches.

The bus stop project became a small example of planning for both present and future needs. Quick solutions are sometimes necessary, but they can be combined with slower changes that improve over time. The tree could not replace the shelter at the beginning, and the shelter could not grow. Together, they created a better result than either one alone.
translation:
病院近くの混雑するバス停では、夏になると利用者が強い日差しの中で待つことがありました。小さな屋根はありましたが、午後の西日にはあまり役立ちません。市は大きな金属屋根を設置しようとしましたが、造園担当者が木も解決策の一部にできないか提案しました。

ただし木を植える場所には地下配管があり、根が歩道を持ち上げたり、成長後に標識を隠したりする可能性があります。小さな木では日陰ができるまで時間もかかります。そこで都市の暑さに強く、適度に早く育ち、根が舗装を傷めにくい種類を選びました。

すぐ日陰が必要なので、市は小型の屋根も設置しました。木は待合場所の西側に植え、成長した時に午後の影が座席側へ伸びるよう位置を決めました。若木の幹を自転車から守る枠を付け、最初の二夏は市職員が定期的に水をやりました。

『屋根があるのに木へ費用をかけるのは無駄』という声や、すぐ涼しくなると期待する声もありました。担当者は、屋根は今日の問題を解決し、木は将来の日陰、舗装温度の低下、街路の快適さへの投資だと説明しました。

五年後、木は十分育ち、待合場所の一部へ広い影を落とすようになりました。暑い日は金属屋根より葉の下の席を選ぶ人も増え、鳥が枝で休むこともありました。

この計画は、現在と将来を同時に考える例になりました。すぐ効く方法が必要な時でも、時間とともに良くなる方法を組み合わせることができます。最初、木は屋根の代わりにならず、屋根は成長しませんでした。しかし二つを合わせることで、どちらか一つより良い結果になったのです。
